newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma says problems solved with Russia.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma says problems solved with Russia.

text.p: President Leonid Kuchma said on Sunday agreement had been achieved with Russia on two issues dogging their post-Soviet relations, division of the Black Sea Fleet and Russian duties on Ukrainian imports.

Kuchma, quoted by Interfax Ukraine news agency, said the accords were the outcome of weekend talks in Moscow with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who is to visit Ukraine next month. But he offered no details.

"We achieved full agreement on both the Black Sea Fleet and trade issues, including the imposition of the tax on Ukrainian imports," Kuchma told Interfax nes agency at a ceremony marking the mass Nazi slaughter of Kiev residents, mostly Jews, at Babi Yar.

Russia's Itar-Tass news agency quoted a government source in Moscow as saying both sides "had moved forward on many issues." But it said scant publicity given to the talks showed it was premature to speak about solving the issues for good.
Ukraine and Russia have concluded several accords on splitting the Fleet's ships since the 1991 collapse of Soviet rule, but major differences persist on how to share out its bases.

Several Russian politicians, including security chief Alexander Lebed, have recently relaunched suggestions that Sevastopol, the Fleet's main base in Ukraine's Crimean peninula is legally and historically Russian territory.

Russia initially intended to introduce a 20 percent "value added tax" on Ukrainian imports from September to guard against what officials say is mass dumping, but postponed it for a month after intensive talks.

A 10 percent tax on sugar imports, denounced by Ukraine as discriminatory, is already in effect. Interfax quoted an official in Uraine's Foreign Trade Ministry as predicting the tax would have little long-term effect on trade with Russia.

A treaty of friendship between the two sides remains unsigned, mainly because of the unresolved Fleet issue. President Boris Yeltsin, now preparing for heart surgery, has postponed a visit to Kiev six times in the past two years.
Kuchma told Interfax a series of accords would be signed during Chernomyrdin's forthcoming visit to Kiev, leaving him and Yeltsin to sign the friendship pact at a later date.
"We have no differences," he said. Kuchma said Chernomyrdin told him that Yeltsin "felt all right. Any operation is a difficult thing. Let's hope it will all go well."
